items.title: Correction limits and osmotic risk
items.contentHtml:
Slow correction of chronic hyponatremia

  • In chronic hyponatremia (>48 hours or unknown) the correction should not exceed 8 mmol/L on any day to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome.
  • Patients at high risk (alcoholism, malnutrition, liver disease) require an even stricter limit: 4-6 mmol/L

items.title: Osmolarity classification
items.contentHtml:
Serum osmolality in hypotonic hyponatremia

  • Hypotonic hyponatremia is defined by a serum osmolality < 275 mOsm/kg of volume and urinary sodium to guide the etiology.
  • Urinary osmolarity helps differentiate between excessive water intake (urinary osmolarity <100 mOsm/kg) and states with ADH present (>100, often >300).

items.title: SIADH diagnostic criteria
items.contentHtml:
Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion

  • The essential criteria of syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion are: hypoosmolarity (<275 mOsm/kg), inappropriately high urinary osmolarity (>100 mOsm/kg, typically >300), urinary sodium >40 mmol/L (with normal salt intake), clinical euvolemia, and absence of hypothyroidism or adrenal insufficiency.
  • The most common cause is ectopic ADH secretion due to neoplasms (small cell lung cancer), lung or neurological diseases, and drugs (antidepressants, carbamazepine).
  • First-line treatment is water restriction (500-1000 mL/day); If it fails, V2 receptor antagonists such as tolvaptan are used (with strict control of correction).

items.foco: Hypovolemic vs euvolemic vs hypervolemic hyponatremia
items.title: Differential diagnosis according to volume
items.contentHtml:
Hypovolemic vs euvolemic vs hypervolemic hyponatremia

  • Hypovolemic hyponatremia: sodium and water losses with water-only replacement (diuretics, vomiting, diarrhea). Urinary sodium <20 mmol/L if extrarenal loss; >20 if renal loss (diuretics, osmotic diuresis).
  • Euvolemic hyponatremia: typically syndrome of inadequate ADH secretion, hypothyroidism or adrenal insufficiency. Urinary sodium >40 mmol/L and urinary osmolarity >100.
  • Hypervolemic hyponatremia: cirrhosis, heart failure, nephrotic syndrome. Urinary sodium <20 mmol/L (except if diuretics). Treatment is sodium and water restriction, plus loop diuretics.
  • The clinical assessment of volume (skin turgor, oral mucosa, jugular venous pressure, edema) is essential for classification.

items.title: Prevention and management
items.contentHtml:
Osmotic demyelination syndrome

  • Osmotic demyelination syndrome (previously called central pontine myelinolysis) is a complication of excessive or rapid correction of chronic hyponatremia, especially if 8 mmol/L is exceeded in 24 hours.
  • Clinically it manifests itself with dysarthria, dysphagia, paraparesis. spasticity, altered level of consciousness and, in severe cases, locked-in syndrome.
  • Risk factors: alcoholism, malnutrition, liver disease, hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia and use of diuretics.
  • If overcorrection is detected (>8 mmol/L/day), the correction should be stopped by administering 5% glucose solution and desmopressin for sodium re-lowering.

items.title: Indications and infusion
items.contentHtml:
Treatment with 3% hypertonic saline solution

  • Indicated in severe symptomatic hyponatremia (seizures, coma, respiratory arrest) and in acute hyponatremia (<48 hours) with moderate-severe symptoms.
  • The initial dose is 100-150 mL of 3% hypertonic saline solution as a bolus. for 10-20 minutes (or 2 mL/kg), which raises serum sodium approximately 2-4 mmol/L immediately.
  • Goal: increase serum sodium 4-6 mmol/L in the first 4-6 hours to reverse symptoms, then stop or reduce the infusion.
  • Monitor serum sodium every 1-2 hours during the infusion to avoid overcorrection. The Adrogué-Madias formula helps predict the change: (Infused Na - Serum Na) / (total body water + 1).

items.title: Calculation of free water deficit
items.contentHtml:
Sodium deficit formula in hypernatremia

  • Hypernatremia reflects a deficit of free water; The formula to estimate the water deficit (in liters) is: Total body water (ACT) × [(serum Na/140) - 1], where ACT = 0.5 × weight (kg) in women and 0.6 × weight in men.
  • Example: 70 kg male with Na=160 mmol/L: deficit = 42 L × [(160/140)-1] = 42 × 0.143 = 6 L.
  • Correction should be slow: reduce serum sodium no more than 10-12 mmol/L in 24 hours to avoid cerebral edema.
  • Administer half of the deficit in the first 24 hours, replenishing with 5% glucose solution or free water orally/enterally.

items.title: Dehydration test and response
items.contentHtml:
Central vs nephrogenic diabetes insipidus

  • Central diabetes insipidus is due to a deficiency of antidiuretic hormone (ADH); nephrogenic refers to renal resistance to ADH.
  • The dehydration test (water deprivation for 4-18 hours) differentiates both: in the central test, urinary osmolarity increases >50% after desmopressin; in nephrogenic diabetes the increase is <10%.
  • In central diabetes insipidus, basal urinary osmolarity is low (<300 mOsm/kg) and after desmopressin it exceeds 600-800 mOsm/kg.
  • Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus can be congenital (mutation of the V2 or aquaporin-2 receptor) or acquired (lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia).

items.foco: Causes of hypernatremia due to loss of free water
items.title: Renal and extrarenal losses
items.contentHtml:
Causes of hypernatremia due to loss of free water

  • Renal losses: central or nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, osmotic diuresis (glucose, mannitol, urea), and loop diuretics that impair the ability to concentrate.
  • Extrarenal losses: excessive sweating (fever, exercise), gastrointestinal losses (osmotic diarrhea, vomiting), and extensive burns.
  • Urinary osmolarity helps locate the site of loss: <300 mOsm/kg suggests diabetes insipidus; >600 mOsm/kg points to extrarenal losses or hypodipsia.
  • In patients with hypodipsia (hypothalamic lesion) or limited access to water, hypernatremia is due to insufficient free water intake.

items.foco: Response to desmopressin in diabetes insipidus
items.title: Test interpretation
items.contentHtml:
Response to desmopressin in diabetes insipidus

  • After administering desmopressin (antidiuretic hormone analogue) subcutaneously or intranasally, urinary osmolarity is measured at 2 and 4 hours.
  • An increase >50% in urinary osmolarity with respect to the value basal indicates complete central diabetes insipidus.
  • An increase <10% indicates nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.
  • In partial central diabetes insipidus, the response is intermediate (10-50%), and can be managed with low doses of desmopressin or with agents that stimulate ADH secretion (chlorpropamide, carbamazepine).

items.foco: Evaluation of urinary sodium and urinary osmolarity
items.title: Laboratory interpretation
items.contentHtml:
Evaluation of urinary sodium and urinary osmolarity

  • In hypotonic hyponatremia, urinary sodium distinguishes: <20 mmol/L suggests effective volume depletion (cirrhosis, heart failure, extrarenal losses); >40 mmol/L suggests syndrome of inadequate ADH secretion or renal losses.
  • Urinary osmolarity <100 mOsm/kg indicates excessive water intake (primary polydipsia, beer potomania); >100 mOsm/kg suggests that antidiuretic hormone is present.
  • In hypernatremia, a urine osmolarity <300 mOsm/kg points to diabetes insipidus; >600 mOsm/kg indicates extrarenal losses or hypodipsia.
  • Urinary sodium in hypernatremia <20 mmol/L suggests extrarenal losses; >20 mmol/L, renal losses (osmotic diuresis, diuretics).

items.foco: Risk of overcorrection and use of desmopressin
items.title: Management of overcorrection
items.contentHtml:
Risk of overcorrection and use of desmopressin

  • Overcorrection is defined as an increase in serum sodium >8 mmol/L in 24 hours (or >10-12 mmol/L in hypernatremia), associated with the risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome.
  • If overcorrection is detected, it should be stopped. hypertonic infusion and administer desmopressin 1-2 mcg intravenously or subcutaneously to stop aqueous diuresis, together with 5% glucose solution to re-lower sodium.
  • In patients with chronic hyponatremia treated with 3% hypertonic saline, prophylactic desmopressin can be administered to avoid overcorrection and control the rate of ascent.
  • Monitor serum sodium every 2 hours during the active correction phase to adjust therapy.
